answer.rationale: Three pieces of inherited memory are directly load-bearing for the current decision, so I want to check that they still reflect the file before I commit. c2 records that the low-cost vendor delivered accurate invoicing and a quick onboarding the last time we moved primary supply there; that bears on whether switching primary now would actually be cheap and low-risk, or whether the savings on paper would be eaten by execution problems. c4 records that the last renewal negotiation moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms when we benchmarked against market rates; that is the mechanism I plan to use this cycle, so I need to be sure the incumbent has historically responded to it rather than stonewalled. c1 records that the incumbent has held integration stable across two renewal cycles with no migration work and no delivery interruption; with the line already at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, that stability is exactly what I cannot afford to lose if the negotiation fails and we have to fall back to the status quo. The finance mandate is an 18% cut to component spend, the primary contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, and I have capacity for one sourcing decision this cycle, so the move has to do real work on cost without putting deliveries at risk. Renewing on the same terms fails the cost objective; switching primary outright to the low-cost vendor (c2) chases the cheapest unit price but concentrates volume with one vendor during a no-buffer run and gives up the integration stability recorded in c1, which is too much delivery risk given the 94% utilization. Adding a second source helps resilience (memory c3) but does not, on its own, close an 18% cost gap before the contract expires. Deferring past quarter end (c5) leaves us exposed on a contract that does not auto-renew, and at 94% utilization even a short lapse is painful. Negotiating terms with the incumbent is the one action that can hit the 18% target on the existing contract timeline while keeping the stable integration (c1) intact; c4 tells me benchmarking against market rates has previously moved this incumbent on price AND payment terms, which is the lever I need to actually achieve an 18% reduction rather than a symbolic one. Before I commit I want to pull the archived source record for c2, c4, and c1 — I will cap at one if forced, and in that case prioritize c4 because it is the direct precedent for the negotiation mechanism I plan to use, with c2 as the fallback benchmark for credible market rates and c1 as the final fallback on delivery-risk continuity.
